items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion
without notice in relation to the death of Malcolm Fraser, former Prime Minister of
Australia.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That this House express its sadness at the passing
on 20 March 2015 of former Australian Prime Minister Rt Hon Malcolm Fraser AC,
CH, GCL, aged 84. Mr Fraser served his country with distinction as Australia’s 22 nd
Prime Minister  from 1975, when he was appointed in a caretaker role following the
shock dismissal of Prime Minister Gough Whitlam by the Governor-General. This was
arguably the most dramatic day in Australia’s political history. Mr Fraser went on to
win the following three elections and served as Prime Minister until 1983. During that
time he made a significant contribution to the strengthening of the Australia -  New
Zealand relationship. It was during his time as Prime Minis ter that Australia and New
Zealand negotiated and signed the Australia and New Zealand Closer Economic
Relations Trade Agreement , commonly known as CER, with its enduri ng legacy of
shared prosperity.
He will also be remembered for his work with the United Nations and humanitarian
agencies. Mr Fraser was a strong opponent of white  minority rule in South Africa and
what was then Rhodesia. He served on a number of UN and C ommonwealth bodies
with a focus on southern Africa , and was president of the foreign aid group CARE
International. Mr Fraser was also an advocate for multiculturalism in Australia and for
indigenous and human rights, overseeing the establishment of the Family Court of
Australia and the National Aboriginal Conference, instituting the position of a federal
ombudsman, and passing the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976. He
also played an influential role in the Commonwealth of Nations. On behalf of New
Zealanders, I would like to express our condolences to his family and to the people of
Australia.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I just rise briefly to support the
motion and to acknowledge and record the New Zealand Labour Party’s condolences at
2480 Obituaries 24 Mar 2015
this time over the loss of Malcolm Fraser, and to note that Malcolm Fraser was elevated
to the role of Prime Minister of Australia in arguably the most controversial of
circumstances. He acquitted himself in that post until he was succeeded by Bob Hawke,
and it was his post -  prime ministerial and post parliamentary career that I think he will
be most remembered for, certainly on this side of the House. He led the Eminent
Persons Group on behalf of the Commonwealth Heads of Government to inquire into
apartheid in South Africa, and he was very much a part of the diplomatic process of
leading the change externally that subsequently led to a genuinely free and democratic
South Africa, which ultimately saw the election of Nelson Mandela as President in the
I saw Malcolm Fraser speaking in Australia, interestingly enough at a trade union
conference, which reflected the political change that I think he underwent. He was a
conservative Prime Minister elected in conservative circumstances who had the
presence of mind and the independence of spirit to question what subsequent
conservative Governments in Australia had done, and he challenged some of the
economic nostrums that certainly the John Howard Government had pursued. He took
up the cudgels of not just fre e trade but fair trade in Australia, and a more
compassionate approach to the people and to economic change and management there.
We note his passing.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: On behalf of the Green Party I offer our
condolences to the friends and family of Malcolm Fraser, and acknowledge the huge
contribution that he made to Australian politics and society. My colleague Russel
Norman described Malcolm Fraser as an outstanding Australi an voice of sanity and
humanity. Throughout his life, he stood up for what was right and championed a very
progressive social agenda, with great concern for those who were the most
marginalised. He was a fierce opponent of apartheid. He helped to form the Gleneagles
Agreement, which insisted that South Africa end apartheid if it wanted to continue to
compete in the Commonwealth Games, and he infamously banned the plane carrying
the Springbok rugby team from refuelling in Australia on its way to New Zealand for
the tour in 1981. He continued this work after leaving Parliament, including chairing the
Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group against apartheid in South Africa.
He had a deep interest in the advancement of indigenous people, and it was his
Government that recognised Aboriginal land rights by establishing the land rights
regime in the Northern Territory. He also established the National Aboriginal
Conference, a national organisation that represented indigenous Australians. His
Government also established the Human Rights Commission. He was a champion of a
multicultural Australia, and he set up the SBS, a channel to provide multilingual
broadcasting for Australia’s migrant community. He was instrumental in Australia
accepting 70,000 Vietnamese refugees displaced by the Viet Nam War, including 2,000
who arrived by boat with no documentation. He also worked to ensure that these
refugees were embraced once they were in Australia. This cause stayed with him for
life, most notably expressed by his quitting the Liberal Party in 2009 after its election ad
portraying asylum seekers swamping Australia. He described the ad as “a throwback to
a racist past, and not just for the Liberal Party but for Australia”.
His legacy also extends to environmental concerns. His Gove rnment prohibited
exploration and drilling for petroleum on the Great Barrier Reef, and later declared the
Great Barrier Reef a marine park. He also banned sand mining on Fraser Island, passed
legislation to create national parks in Australia, and under hi s leadership the first
Australian sites were placed on the World Heritage List. His Government also enacted
the Whale Protection Act, ending whaling in Australia, and it achieved greater
protection for Australian wildlife. Malcolm Fraser was also staunch o n climate change.
Back in 1980 he said: “The planet’s capacity to support its people is being irreversibly
24 Mar 2015 Obituaries 2481
reduced by the destruction and degradation of the biosphere, and the need to understand
the problem and take corrective action is becoming urgent.” O ver 30 years later he put
his name to action on climate change, saying: “The overwhelming body of scientific
evidence supports the need for change. Many countries are well ahead of Australia. We
need to act or we will fall further behind.”
When asked what he considered his badge of honour, there was a list of
administrative law reform, including establishing the Human Rights Commission, and
he said: “Because they all go to how Governments treat its people.” Thank you.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I rise on
behalf of New Zealand First to support the motion. It would appear that we are marking
the end of the generation of Western political leaders from the 1970s. Malcolm Fraser’s
death follows that of the other two major players in Australia’s biggest ever political
crisis. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: It is a respectful motion for a man who was important in
politics. It is a shame that some members of the House do not feel that way, but New
Zealand First does and does not take this lightly. Mr Fraser is one of the last political
players in what was Australia’s biggest ever political crisis, with Gough Whitlam
passing last year and Sir John Kerr passing in 1991.
Malcolm Fraser’s most famous quote is considered by some to be: “Life is not meant
to be easy.” One might say that this encapsulates his belief in self -discipline and
individual sacrifice, and that it sums  up nicely the event that will for ever dominate his
legacy as a master of detail. In 1975 the Liberal majority in the Australian Senate
refused to pass Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam’s money bill. This paralysed
Australia’s Government. The tipping poi nt came when Whitlam refused to resign or to
call a general election, which saw the Governor -General, Sir  John Kerr, exercise his
rarely used reserve p owers to dismiss Whitlam’s Labo r Government. Malcom Fraser
became caretaker Prime Minister that day, 11 N ovember 1975, which is of course
Armistice Day. A general election was called for 13 December of that year, and despite
the controversy of Whitlam’s dismissal, Fraser led the Liberal - Country Party coalition
to the largest victory in Australian history, t aking 30 seats off Labo r to secure a 55 -seat
majority.
While Fraser repudiated some of Whitlam’s initiatives; he extended others —
confounding his opponents and their perception of him as an aloof, landed grazier. As
we have already heard, from 1975 until hi s 1993 defeat by Labor’s Bob Hawke, he
established the Australian Family Court and the Federal Court of Australia. He also
gave the Northern Territory self -government and passed Aboriginal land rights. He
followed our much earlier lead in New Zealand by creating federal ombudsmen. He also
ended the mining of mineral sands from Fraser Island and declared 36,000 square
kilometres of the Great Barrier Reef off Cairns as a marine park. Yet he was also not
scared to use mineral extraction where it made sense, and these resources boomed under
his leadership, helping to propel the Australian economy.
Malcolm Fraser was touched by the plight of Vietnamese refugees and made great
efforts to expand that refugee programme —something he continued with after leaving
office. Socially, he introduced family allowances paid to mothers and oversaw the
decision to build a new Parliament House in Canberra. Internationally, he supported
anti-apartheid boycotts against South Africa, and given the state of global farming in the
1970s, he also called for a global common fund to stabilise commodity prices. Fraser
was an economic traditionalist, yet together with that other giant of politics, Sir Robert
Muldoon, they negotiated and agreed closer economic relations between our two
2482 Obituaries 24 Mar 2015
countries. This remains our most important trade agreement, proving that sensible trade
agreements based on common sense do work.
Malcolm Fraser was born in 1930 in Melbourne and grew up on the family farm. He
graduated from Oxford University in 1952, working as  a grazier before becoming in
1955, at the age of 25, the youngest federal member of Parliament. He would serve for
28 years. An imposingly tall figure at 6 feet, 4 inches, in 1956 he married Tamara
Beggs, who survives him, and together they had four children —Mark, Angela, Hugh,
and Phoebe. Our sympathies go to them, their families, and the Australian people.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I want to associate myself with
the r emarks that have been made by others paying tribute to John Malcolm Fraser,
Australia’s late Prime Minister, who died at the end of last week. I am not going to
quote extensively from Wikipedia in doing so, but I do want to observe that Malcolm
Fraser was a man of extraordinary contrasts —the conservative Prime Minister, whose
record is one of social reform; the patrician country squire from Wannon in Victoria,
who was a career politician from the age of 25, but who abruptly resigned from
Parliament upon losing the election in 1983, to return to his roots.
He was the man who in recent years established a strong following in social media
with his comments on all ranges of issues as recently as the last couple of weeks on the
international situation, the environment, Australian politics, and always from the
perspective of some common sense, some good judgment, and a real heart and
compassion for those who were adversely or marginally affected by decisions of
Governments. The interesting thing to me about Malcom Fraser was given the
circumstances of his arrival in office, where he was labelled for many years as Kerr’s
cur by Gough Whitlam, the two went on to become very firm friends in their post -
political careers, who apparently often met to lament the state of their respective
political parties subsequent to their departures.
New Zealand has lost a good friend. CER was an initiative of the Fraser
Government. The “Nareen agreement”, entered into on his country property, is another
enduring mark of cooperation betw een our two countries. It is appropriate for this
Parliament to pay tribute to a great Australian leader. It is appropriate that we share our
sympathy with his family, his former colleagues, his friends, and mark the greatness of
his contribution to his nation.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Far be it from me to give another exhaustive
account of this great man’s life. However, what I would like to do is pay tribute to one
particular aspect of his prime ministership and career: he changed the culture and the
face of Australia by welcoming over 200,000 immigrants to Australia during his time as
Prime Minister. That is a statement about how countries like our own and Australia
should regard the world not as something we are afraid of but as something in which we
stand tall and welcome immigrants  to our shores. And on that note, I would like today
to share my condolences with our Australian cousins on the loss of a great and tall
eucalyptus. Thank you.
Motion agreed to.
Hon Lee Kuan Yew GCMG, CH

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion
without notice in relation to the death of Hon Lee Kuan Yew, the former Prime Minister
of Singapore.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That this House express its sadness at the passing
on 23 March 2015 of former Prime Minister of Singapore, Hon Lee Kuan Yew  GCMG,
24 Mar 2015 Obituaries 2483
CH, aged 91. As one of S ingapore’s founding fathers, Mr Lee led Singapore to
independence in 1965 and remained its Prime Minister until 1990. Due to his
unwavering determination and vision, Mr Lee guided Singapore’s growth and
development, making it the world leader among small countries that it is today.
Mr Lee was a long -time friend of New Zealand and a supporter of New Zealand’ s
role in South- east Asia. He was also instrumental in establishing the Association of
South-east Asian Nations, ASEAN. New Zealand and ASEAN celebrate o ur 40 th
anniversary this year. On behalf of all New Zealanders , we would like to express our
condolences to Mr Lee’s family and the people of Singapore, who have lost a father
with his passing.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Can I join with the Acting Prime
Minister on behalf of Labour in expressing our condolences to the people of Singapore
and, in particular, to his family and his son, the current Prime Minister of Singapore, on
his passing. Lee Kuan Yew was an extraordinary figure. I remember when he gave a
speech on television in 1965—and I think I was a 12- year-old; a child at that time —he
spoke with such power and emotion about why he was t aking Singapore out of
Malaysia, and dec ades later I still remember that as the first political speech that ever
impacted on me in that way.
I remember the Prime Minister for another reason, and that was when I had dinner
with Lee Kuan Yew at the Shangri -La Dialogue in 2008. I explained to the then mentor
Minister that my mother was a great admirer of his. He looked at me somewhat
quizzically and said: “Why would that be the case?”, and I explained that in 1977, as a
student who had gone 6 years without a haircut, passing through Singapore I was  given
my first haircut by the customs officials at the airport as the price of entry. My mother
congratulated him on achieving something that nobody else had been able to do for
years before that time.
There are aspects of Lee Kuan Yew that all of us wou ld immensely admire. He
turned a Third World country into a First World country with a higher per capita
standard of living than we enjoy in this country. He dealt effectively with corruption, he
built a first- class education system, and he transformed the  living standards and grew
the GDP of that country 15 times between 1960 and 1980. There was, however, another
side to Lee Kuan Yew, which he himself admitted when he was being interviewed in
2010, and that was that he was a very authoritarian figure, he l ocked up his opponents,
and he cracked down on the media. He admitted that he had done some bad things in his
time, and that was the other side, which, if we were to be fair in our memory of Lee
Kuan Yew, we would also acknowledge. But today, in particular , we remember him as
a man who was a strong leader, who gave Singapore an influence totally
disproportionate to its size, and created a better country for his fellow countrymen and
women.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Green Party pays tribute to the passing of
Lee Kuan Yew , former Prime Minister of Singapore. Our condolences go out to his
family, on a personal basis, and also to his son, the current Prime Minister, Lee Hsien
Loong, on behalf of the nation.
Lee Kuan Yew  was recognised as the founding father of his nation. He was a
formidable figure in world politics. When Singapore gained independence in 1965 he
began work on what has been called the economic miracle. He transformed the small
island nation into a modern and prosperous place of the 21 st century. He did so with a
raft of re gulation, a strong emphasis on g overnment, and a mix of private and State
capitalism.
As with every country, the rise of modern Singapore did not come without som e
cost. Lee was quoted as saying that he had sacrificed his life for Singapore. He
2484 Obituaries 24 Mar 2015
maintained a close rei n on the country and its people in the interests of growing the
country in the way he envisioned it. His tenure, of course, was not without its
controversy. In the resulting debate over Asian values not so long ago was a substantive
and interesting exchange with the West. We in the Green Party, naturally, have our
views, yet we acknowledge the change that was wrought in Singapore, and we
appreciate his l eadership, his determination, and his vision for a better life for his
countrymen and women. Today we join the citizens of Singapore in remembrance of
their leader, whom history will regard as a giant on the political landscape of our times.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. When I
first came into this House 3 years ago, one of the first things that was sent to my office
were these books on the life and times of Lee Kuan Yew, and part of the reason for
that—and I thank the sender —was that the Rt Hon Winston Peters highly, highly,
highly respects Lee Kuan Yew and what he did for his country. So I know that the Rt
Hon Winston Peters, if he were not otherwise working hard in another area of New
Zealand, would wish to be here to take this call.
The sympathies of New Zealand First, but especially of the Rt Hon Winston Peters,
go out to Lee Kuan Yew’s children and to the people of Singapore. He was truly one of
the gr eats when it came to belief in his people and in what they could achieve in a
nation with very few resources. He gained the respect of his people and he gained the
respect of the majority of the informed world for his visionary plans for a small island
nation.
I know that the Rt Hon Winston Peters had the opportunity to meet and spend some
time with him. Only yesterday the Rt Hon Winston Peters wrote that it was one of the
most valuable meetings he could ever have had. In closing, as we acknowledge his
passing, Lee Kuan Yew’s given name in Mandarin means “light and brightness”. We
would respectfully suggest that the world is a little bit less light and a little bit less
bright for his passing. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: High on the walls of St Paul’s
Cathedral is the inscription “If you seek his monument, look around you”. It applies to
Sir Christopher Wren, but it could equally apply to Lee Kuan Yew, because he was  a
man whose monument is modern Singapore—simple and straightforward.
I recall meeting him at a dinner in Wellington some years ago, where he described
the Singapore story very simply, very bluntly, and very basically. He said: “At the end
of the war we were a set of stinking, rotten pieces of territory, with no natural resources.
We had been plundered by the enemy during the war. We had no future. We either gave
up or we got stuck in and tried to do something. And we looked around our region and
we saw two  big fat countries, Australia and New Zealand, and we decided to emulate
them. And that is what we have done over the last 50 years.”

items.speaker: And then he finished the discussion by saying
items.text: “And you know what —there are still
two big fat countries in our region”, which was a challenge that I think he was making
to Australia and to New Zealand about where we are in terms of social and economic
progress. “We have come from nowhere to be an icon for many throughout the world.
What have you done in your country?”. And I think that really summed up—when I
read the biographies and saw the documentaries about Lee Kuan Yew—what was, at his
essence, a fundamentally very simple and humble man who knew that you have to use
your talents and your abilities to the best advantage in your country. And he did that in
Singapore, and he did that in a way that has made his country truly one, for him —in his
lifetime, obviously—to be proud of, for his successor to be proud of, and one, I think,
about which there are lessons that we can learn as well.
So we mourn not just his passing, we mourn his inspiration, we mourn his leadership,
and we wish him, obviously, every respect, and we wish his country well as it seeks to
24 Mar 2015 Obituaries 2485
get used to life without its mentor -Minister, its founding Prime Minister, and its great
leader.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Abe Lincoln once said that “Nearly all men
can stand adversity, but if you would like to test a man’s character, give him power.”
Lee Kuan Yew was an extraordinary man who ruled in a constitutional arrangement that
I suspect very few, if any, in this House would have a lot of patience or support for.
And, undoubtedly, at times he did misuse and abuse his power, at the cost of what we
would regard as normal civil liberties.
But all of that is only a preamble to paying tribute to what he did for Singapore, a
country that in the 1960s was a recipient of foreign aid from New Zealand and today has
twice the GDP per capita that we do. It is a tribute n ot only to the great man, Lee Kuan
Yew, but also to the approach he took to open markets, free trade, a flexible labour
market, and tolerable taxes that have allowed the people of Singapore, who had no
natural resources to speak of, to become so prosperous . So on behalf of the ACT Party I
would like to join with other leaders in paying tribute to a great man and in wishing all
the best for the people of Singapore in this time of sorrow. Thank you.
Motion agreed to.
State and Social Housing—Sale of Housing Stock
1. TIM MACINDOE (National—Hamilton West) to the Minister responsible for

items.speaker: HNZC
items.text: What are the objectives of the Government’s social housing reform
programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The programme will
assist more people with serious housing need by delivering more social houses where
they are most needed. The Government has set out five objectives: to ensure people who
need housing support from the Government can get it; to help social housing tenants to
independence, as appropriate; to ensure that the properties for social housing are the
right size and in the right place; to help increase the supply of afforda ble housing; and
to encourage more diverse ownership of social housing.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What steps is the Government taking under the social housing
reform programme to deliver on these objectives?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: A number of steps. We will purchase 3,000 more social
housing places over the next 3 years, and are currently in the process of purchasing 300
of them in Auckland. We will accelerate Housing New Zealand builds and disposals.
We will open up access to income -related rents to the community housing sector. We
are committed to 5,000 tenancy reviews over the next 2 years to support tenants back
into independence. Building is under way in the Tāmaki  regeneration of up to 3,000
houses. We are committed to the transfer of 1,000 to 2,000 houses to the community
sector in the next 12 to 18 months.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to get more social housing to
where it is most needed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Around one -third of Housing New Zealand houses —$18.7
billion worth of them—are the wrong size and in the wrong place. Just, for instance, 45
percent of current tenancies are for one single person —45 percent of our houses are
occupied by one person —but only 9 percent of the housing stock has one bedroom. So
we have thousands of single tenants in three -bedroom and two- bedroom houses.
Housing New Zealand is making good progress in rebalancing its portfolio. Last year it
2486 Oral Questions 24 Mar 2015
sold 600 houses, mostly in areas of low demand, and it is currentl y building around 700
new houses this year.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: Does the Minister stand by his statement in reference to the social
housing reform programme that “These other agencies are having a thorough look and
are telling us a whole lot about our business we didn’t know.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. State housing has been run by a Government monopoly
for, I think, at least 70 years, and because there has been no pressure to compete or to do
a better job, there have been significant aspects of that that were not clear to previous
Governments or to this Government. But in this whole process of social housing reform,
we are finding things out, like the fact that although 45 percent of our tenants are single-
person households, only 9 percent of our houses are single-bedroom households.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: Has his Government not released the findings of the warrant of fitness
trial, which includes 20 State houses in the Northland electorate, because the results
would show that these houses are falling apart around thousands of vulnerable tenants,
or is he waiting for these other agencies to tell the public what a disgrace these State
houses are in?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The results of that trial will be released in  due course, but
the member does highlight a reasonable issue. Pretty much every MP knows, if they are
doing their constituent work, that this large -scale Government agency could have been
doing a better job. I am pleased to say that Housing New Zealand’s performance is
improving pretty rapidly now, and I think the main reason is that there are others
showing up where they could do it better.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What examples can the Minister provide of a community housing
provider supporting the s ocial housing reforms but opting not directly to buy former
State houses on its own in the immediate future?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I am aware that the Salvation Army yesterday
confirmed that it supports the Government’s policy to have community organisations
involved in the management of social housing, and that under the current policy it will
continue to provide and expand its social houses. It confirmed that it is keen to pursue
housing partnerships between itself, the Government, and other groups, but it did say
that it would not take part in these particular transactions. I am pleased to say that there
is widespread interest in the Government housing policy, because unlike the Labour
Party, everyone else in New Zealand thinks it can be done better.
State and Social Housing—Sale of Housing Stock
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statements that his plan to sell  state houses “is not about selling to
developers” and he would be “amazed” if the likes of the Salvation Army were hesitant
to get involved?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, the social housing reforms
are about better outcomes for our tenants, many of whom have been locked into
dependency for decades when Governments have done very little to assist them to
housing or economic independence. The Salvation Army yesterday  said it is keen to
pursue housing partnerships between itself and the Government and others. In fact, I am
advised that it is in the process right now of registering as a community housing
provider, which will, of course, give it access to income -related rents for the many
hundreds of seriously needy tenants whom it currently looks after. I am sure the
Salvation Army will welcome access to a larger subsidy for New Zealanders in serious
housing need.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Is it correct that he is c onsidering a sweetheart deal for private
developers, with measures including selling the houses below book value, offering
24 Mar 2015 Oral Questions 2487
subsidies, allowing houses to be rented at market rates, or allowing them to be sold into
the private market?

items.speaker: Hon B ILL ENGLISH
items.text: As a result of the first opportunity in 70 years for many
people to have an opinion and to participate in better housing for the most needy New
Zealanders, we have heard all of those ideas. We are going through a process of
working with them and listening to them, because we all have a common purpose to do
a better job for the tenants. The transactions that had been proposed, however, will be
run on a commercial and competitive basis.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Was today’s New Zealand Herald  editorial correct when it said his
policy “amounts to a subsidy, leaving taxpayers out of pocket. And it raises the question
of the whole point of the exercise.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, but the New Zealand Herald may be interested to know
that the Government values its houses currently as if it is a developer. It values them as
if it can get the highest price for an individual house on the day and, of course, social
housing providers who are more focused on looking after the tenants do n ot believe that
those valuations are correct —that as social houses they are not there to capture the full
capital gain and that the issue is precisely the opposite of the one the New Zealand
Herald thinks that it is.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Which of  these community housing experts is wrong and why:
Major Campbell Roberts, who said of the housing sell -off: “I don’t there’s been enough
thinking gone into it.”; or Property Institute chief executive officer, Ashley Church, who
said: “If a large, credible, social agency like The Salvation Army thinks that the  current
proposal is too risky—it’s unlikely that any other group is going to be any more willing
to pick it up.”; or, thirdly, the Iwi Leaders Forum housing spokesperson, Sonny Tau,
who said: “I don’t think it’s a good policy.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, two of those three have been knocking on my door for
3 years telling us to hurry up. The iwi leaders group has been criticising the
Government for taking too long to work out the details of how to do these transactions.
So we have every confidence that there is widespread interest in a once- in-a generation
opportunity to redevelop communities that have suffered from the blight of mismanaged
State housing and whose tenants have been neglected by Governments that did not
support them into independence. Increasingly, the Labour Party members are about the
only people who believe that the way it is being done now is perfect.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: In light of that answer, then, is Major Campbell Roberts wrong when
he says the policy will not “improve the lives and living conditions of State tenants.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I believe that he is wrong. But I do not believe that is
the Salvation Army’s views, frankly; otherwise, it would not have invested 5 years in
assisting the Government to develop the policy. Major Campbell Roberts was in the
initial advisory group. He has been supportive and testing about the policy for 5 years. I
respect his view, but on that one I differ from him.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What reports has the Prime Minister seen supporting the
Government’s social housing reform programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have seen one that is a pretty good description of the
possibilities: “We need large- scale urban developments backed by private sector
developers and community housing organisations. Such developments cannot happen
without the Government playing a role. Private sector developers will invest and do
what they do best —designing and building great places for people, and there is a vital
role for community providers to add affordable housing.” That is a description of what
the policy could be from Phil Twyford—the Labour housing spokesman.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: It is 31 for 2 and time is marching on. We need to get a move on.
After telling the House last week that “there is not a housing crisis”, is it not true that
2488 Oral Questions 24 Mar 2015
not only does New Zealand have a social housing crisis and a housing affordability
crisis but now the Government has a housing policy crisis as well?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: What we know with the track record of the Labour Party is
that as soon as it starts calling it a crisis, it comes right. The manufacturing crisis
disappeared pretty much the day Labour christened it that way. No, I disagree with all
those comments. We have a once-in-a generation opportunity to improve the lives of the
most seriously needy New Zealanders who have been neglected by past Governments in
housing that was of low  quality. This Government is going to change it with the
assistance of many hundreds, if not thousands, of other people in New Zealand who
want the same thing.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why is the Government wasting so much time and public money on
this convoluted policy that will not do an ounce of good rather than just getting on with
the job and building more houses for Kiwi families in need?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, of course, it is doing both. We are not just dealing
with the shor t-term issue of more supply on the ground faster —and Housing New
Zealand can become a major supplier of that under these reforms —we are also dealing
with the longer -term issue of people locked into long -term welfare dependency, or , in
some cases, underservicing of their need, in a system that focused on houses rather than
people. We are happy to be the party bringing in a policy that focuses on the people
who need housing, rather than the Labour Party’s focus on the State houses.
State and Social Housing—Sale of Housing Stock
3. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister responsible for

items.speaker: HNZC
items.text: Can he rule out selling Housing New Zealand- owned homes to private
developers; if not, will any sale be cont ingent on developers housing low -income or
vulnerable tenants in those homes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I cannot rule that
out. Housing New Zealand in the last year sold 600 houses, and probably quite a
number of those were sold to private developers. But anyone who wants to buy State
houses that have low -income and vulnerable tenants in them will need to register as a
community housing provider and meet the criteria set out in the regulations.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How is it “perfectly logical”, as he has said, to sell a large slice of
our $18 billion State home asset for cheap so property deve lopers can make a profit
from it?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the first place, Housing New Zealand has an ongoing
sales policy, and often it is selling houses that we do not need or that are in the wrong
place, or some of them have just become u nsuitable to be lived in and cannot be
upgraded at reasonable cost. In respect of the transactions that are coming up over the
next 6 months or so, there is a process of testing what the real values of those houses
are. For instance, many community providers believe those houses are not up to date on
maintenance, and therefore are overvalued when they are valued as if they can be sold
for the best price on the day in the location that they are in. Those are exactly the things
we are having discussions about over the next few months.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister cancel his plans if it turns out that property
developers will buy State homes only if they do not have to house low -income or
vulnerable tenants in them, given his statement today  that the purpose of this plan is to
increase the supply of social housing and assist more people?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Neither property developers nor community housing
providers are compelled to buy houses off the Government. If they do not want to do
that—if they do not want to manage the tenants or own the stock, which may be the
wrong size in the wrong place —then they certainly do not have to do that. But we are
24 Mar 2015 Oral Questions 2489
finding that there is an opportunity to work with a whole range of groups to do a better
job, particularly in those locations where there is a high density of State housing and
there is an opportunity to redevelop a sense of aspiration in those communities. If
property developers can supply their expertise to do that, well, we are  not going to turn
them away, that is for sure, but it will have to be lined up with people who have the
skills to manage tenants and redevelop communities.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Was the Minister suggesting earlier that the Salvation Army was
lying when it said, when it rejected the State house sell -off programme, that it will not
improve people’s lives?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is the member who is misrepresenting the Salvation Army.
It did not reject the programme; what it said was  that at this stage it does not want to
participate in those particular transactions. In fact, the Salvation Army has been an
advocate for change, and I am a bit surprised to hear the so -called radical Greens
arguing for the status quo, as if State housing in New Zealand is done so perfectly well
that it cannot be done any better. That is a ridiculous position, and the only people the
Greens share it with are the Labour Party members.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why is his Government—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I ask the member to start again, please.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why is his Government so hell -bent on transferring New Zealand’s
public resources, assets like power companies and now our State homes, to private
business, regardless of how bad this extremist policy is for New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In respect of State housing, the policy that has been bad for
New Zealanders is the one that , for 50 years, has focused on who owns the house. The
policy that is going to be much better for New Zealanders is one that recognises the
dignity of tenants and the aspirations they have for independence and a better life, and
that allows communities to redevelop themselves when they have been blighted by the
policies supported by the Greens and Labour. We are not in favour of the status quo; we
want to change it. Labour and the Greens are the last people in New Zealand who think
that long -term State housing is the best we can do for Kiwi citizens. It is not.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am just waiting for the Hon Annette King.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that the only group to benefit from his fire
sale will be property developers as the taxpayer loses a large asset, the Government will
pay more to these property developers through income -related rent subsidies, and
vulnerable families will still have no guarantee of a decent home?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not agree with that. The beneficiarie s of this policy
will be, first and foremost, the tenants, who will find themselves getting Government
support that recognises their dignity and aspirations and shows a path to independence.
Lots of other low -income families will benefit too because the Go vernment is the most
inefficient user of land in all our urban markets, and through this process we will see the
redevelopment and supply of that land to the lower -income market. That member
supports planning policies that have driven poverty in low and mi ddle income
households by driving up the cost of housing. It is time the Greens changed their
policies.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is this not the perfect deal for property developers —National will
give away these homes for cheap along with guaranteed taxpayer -funded income
streams and no obligation to house needy people; if so, how is this not the sale of the
century?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I just disagree with the member. It would be worth her while
reconsidering the role of property deve lopers. The Greens support smart growth that
limits the supply of land, which in the Auckland market has virtually dried up the
2490 Oral Questions 24 Mar 2015
supply of lower-value housing to that market. Those policies have had more impact on
inequality than any other policy in New Zea land for low and middle income
households. Why the Greens support that poverty-inducing policy is beyond me.
Free-trade Agreements—New Zealand - South Korea
4. ALASTAIR SCOTT (National —Wairarapa) to the Minister of Trade: What
progress has the Government made in opening up export markets for our regional
economies?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Good progress, just like the
Black Caps this afternoon. Yesterday the New Zealand -  Korea free- trade agreement
was signed in Seoul, Korea, by our Minister of Trade and his Korean counterpart. Upon
ratification, the free -trade agreement will ensure that nearly half of New Zealand’s
exports to Korea will be immediately tariff -free, and then will progressively remove
tariffs on 98 percent of total exports. The impact of tariffs is twofold. New Zealand
exporters pay a high cost in tariffs, and tariffs also substantially  reduce the volume of
our exports into markets. Both of these problems combine to reduce the availability and
competitiveness of New Zealand products. Tariff removal is therefore a key focus of the
Business Growth Agenda target to grow our exports, and com prehensive free- trade
agreements like the Korean free -trade agreement and others are an important part of
that.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: How do free -trade agreements like the one signed with Korea
yesterday help grow regional economics like, for example, Northland?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Most of our regional economies rely strongly on the
performance of the primary sector, and it is the primary sector that has most to gain by
the removal or reduction of heavy tariffs. If you look speci fically at Northland,
Northland is the second- largest supplier of avocados to Korea from New Zealand, with
the Northland region responsible for 37 percent of them. The Korean free -trade
agreement will eliminate the 30 percent tariff on the import of avocados into Korea.
Kiwifruit is another important industry in Northland. New Zealand exports a lot of
kiwifruit to Korea. The tariff is 45 percent. Under the Korean free -trade agreement the
tariff on kiwifruit exports will be reduced to zero over the next 5 ye ars, and so it goes
on, with forestry, dairy, and so on. Free -trade agreements like the one with Korea are
critically important for improving growth in places like Northland, as they provide more
jobs, higher wages, and opportunities for young people.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Does the Minister believe that the Korean free- trade agreement
will actually be of any benefit to the dairying economy of the Northland region when it
will take 10 years to reach a final tariff -free milk power quota of just 2,000 tonnes —
0.13 percent of our current exports —with anything over that amount permanently
subject to a tariff of 176 percent?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do believe it will, because in a number of key tariff lines
great progress has been made. For example, with cheddar cheese we have got an
equivalent deal with that of the US and a better deal that Australia’s, and that is very
important for competition in Korea. If you look at infant formula and at butter, for
example, all those higher -value products have got very good tariff elimination. If the
member is suggesting that is not a good thing for Northland, I would be very surprised
indeed.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: What support has he seen for the Korea free -trade agreement and for
reducing costs on New Zealand’s primary sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Support for the free -trade agreement, particularly from the
primary sector, has been very positive. As I said, the Korean free -trade agreement
eliminates the 40 percent tarif f on beef, the 22.5 percent tariff on sheepmeat, the 45
24 Mar 2015 Oral Questions 2491
percent tariff on kiwifruit, the 30 percent tariff on avocados, and the 89 percent tariff on
butter. Despite this, I have also seen a curious media report that the Korean free -trade
agreement does “no  favours to New Zealand farmers”. There is also, in fact, draft
legislation—before this House shortly —that would have the effect of torpedoing the
Korean free-trade agreement and a number of other trade agreements we are currently
negotiating. The origin o f that comment and that legislation, and the person who wants
to kill off jobs and growth in the Northland electorate, is the same Winston Peters who
is standing in the by-election.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Is the Minister satisfied with the terms negotiated under the Korea
free-trade agreement when the tariff on New Zealand beef under this agreement will be
40 percent but the tariff imposed by the Koreans on American beef is just 32 percent?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The tariffs un der this agreement are declining across a
whole range of areas, as I just detailed in my previous answer, including in the areas of
sheepmeat and beef. It eliminates the 40 percent tariff on beef, and these are good things
for the New Zealand primary secto r. For the member and his colleagues to suggest that
it is not beneficial suggests that they are literally not focused on what is important to
New Zealand farmers and, frankly, Northland farmers.
Resource Management Act Reforms—Land Use in Northland
5. DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) to the Minister for the Environment : Does he
agree with the Northland Regional Council’s 2012 State of the Environment Report that
“large areas of land with prime soils suited for agriculture and horticultural production
continues to be subdivided for lifestyle blocks and urban development”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, but the report also
said that it was not a regionally significant issue, and they decided to not include
specific provisions for protecting such soils in their proposed regional policy statement.
This Government supports the growth of Northland’s agricultural and horticultural
industries, with initiatives like opening up trade and providing funding to support
Northland irrigation initiatives. Our plans for Northland horticulture do not include the
option of legalising marijuana, as proposed yesterday by Winston Peters.
Denis O ’Rourke: Can the Minister give an assurance that the proposed reforms
announced in his speech of 21 January 2015 on overhauling the Resource Management
Act will not exacerbate housing development on prime agricultural land in Northland?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I welcome the fact that building consent numbers in
Northland have grown over the last 3 years, showing an increased level of confidence. I
also welcome the fact that many landowners in Northland are converting over to
products like avocados, and the good work of the Korean free -trade agreement is going
to enable greater wealth. We are a party that believes the best choices about land use are
actually made by the landowners themselv es, and our Resource Management Act
reforms will be good for Northland by giving those landowners the freedom to be able
to use their land profitably.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What specific initiatives has the Government taken that would support
the growth of Northland’s agricultural and horticultural industries?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The Northland Regional Council has indicated two
particular areas in which it is working with the Government to advance the Northland
economy. The first of those is a real concern that too much of the prime land in
Northland is tied up in the complexities of the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act, and they are
very keen to work with the Minister for Māori Development, my colleague Chris
Finlayson, and the Government to reform that Act to ensure that more of that productive
land can produce more exports and wealth f or Northland. The Northland Regional
Council indicated its second priority was in respect of water, and quite recently the
2492 Oral Questions 24 Mar 2015
Minister for Primary Industries has provided funding for the Northland region to be able
to expand irrigation and expand the exports from that region, although I accept we do
not share New Zealand First’s enthusiasm for growing marijuana.
Denis O’Rourke: Are the proposed Resource Management Act reforms, which are
aimed at freeing up more land for housing, at the expense of agricultural land, consistent
with the Government’s aim of doubling agricultural production by 2025; if so, how?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Members on this side of the House want a Resource
Management Act that is going to protect the enviro nment, but also ensure that
economies like Northland are able to grow. The consistent message I have had from
organisations like Federated Farmers in Northland, and the business associations in
Northland, is that Resource Management Act reform is pivotal t o unlocking the
economic opportunities in Northland, and that is why members on this side of the House
are committed to that reform.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Is the Minister aware of historic reports of subdivision of
productive land, including as long as 70 years ago in St Mary’s Bay?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I do understand that one of the candidates in Northland has
a very intense interest in St Mary’s Bay and what might occur there. Our candidate in
Northland is far more interested i n the practical job opportunities for the people of
Northland.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is a point of order, and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Could you please clarify how the answer had anything to do with
the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear from the Hon Gerry Brownlee.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Well, the question related directly to St Mary’s Bay and was
answered directly about St Mary’s Bay. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume her seat. The question asked for
any historic reports on the subdivision of land around St Mary’s Bay. That is a question
that is quite legitimate. I could tell where it was going, but it was a legitimate question
to be asked in this House, and that is why the member then addressed it.
Roading, Northland—Bridges Upgrade
6. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: What advice, if any, did he receive from the Treasury on the Government
policy to double-lane ten Northland bridges?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: None.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: When was the proposal to fund the 10 bridges first raised with
him as finance Minister?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I could not give the member that detail. I would have to go
back—it may not even be in a diary, actually. But it is a proposal by a political party,
and you would not expect Treasury to be costing it.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why did he not seek advice from Treasury about the expenditure
of $70 million?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Because I follow the rules, and if I had not followed them,
that member would be asking me questions about why I had as ked Treasury for costing
information about it.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How does he reconcile his repeated statements that he stands for
fiscal responsibility, when he is prepared to throw $70 million at the bridges, seven of
24 Mar 2015 Oral Questions 2493
which have never even been mentioned by the New Zealand Transport Agency, and he
does not even bother to get any advice on them?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member is a wee bit ahead of the circumstances. A
political party has made an undertaking in an election, t he Northland by -election.
Whether it can be executed may well depend on the outcome of that election and how
far and how deep Labour is wil ling to bury its candidate, who I understand is popular,
and has a lot of people who could help her out, but Labour insists—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not see any ministerial responsibility.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer, where he said that the policy to build the
10 bridges may or may not be executed, can he confirm to this House t hat there will be
the 10 bridges completed under a National Government?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is certainly National’s view, but in order to achieve a
majority in this House you have to work with other parties. So when we have a by -
election we do not know exactly what the result will be. We may find ourselves
working with different people who have a different view. But it is certainly the
Government’s position that Northland needs the bridges. We have made that
undertaking and we will follow through on it.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is the fact that he sought no advice on spending $70 million proof
that he and his Government are prepared to abuse their power in what John Armstrong
called a “Brazen, shameless, cynical and more than a little desperate” attempt to cling
on to the Northland seat?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I find that people’s cynicism about the bridges in Northland
is directly proportional to how far away they live from them. I invite that member, or
John Armstrong, to go and stand on the bridge in Matakohe and just see what it is like
on the one-lane bridge on a main road. Yes, we believe the bridges should be built and,
as I said to the member before, if I had asked Treasury for advice he would be accusing
me of breaking the rules around election promises.
Accelerated Regional Roading Programme—Progress
7. SARAH DOWIE (National—Invercargill) to the Minister of Transport : What
progress has the Government made on its Accelerated Regional Roading Programme?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Great progress is being made.
First up, the Government is committing up to $80 million to accelerate five critically
important regional projects in Northland, the East Coast, Taranaki, Canterbury, and
Otago as but a few examples. Work is already under way on the East Coast to improve,
and make safer, opportunities for passing on Sta te Highway 35 north of Gisborne at
Panikau Hill and Wallis Hill. Work is also under way on the reconstruction of the
historically dangerous Normanby overbridge in South Taranaki. I visited it with my
colleague the Hon Chester Borrows. And, of course, work on the Akarama curves
realignment project in Northland is under way. Once completed, these projects and
others will provide safer and more reliable road journeys for motorists in the regions.

items.speaker: Sarah Dowie
items.text: How will the Accelerated Regional Roa ding programme improve
single-lane bridging infrastructure in the regions?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, bridges are important. That is why the Accelerated
Regional Roading programme includes a number —quite a number—of bridge upgrades
as but  a couple of examples show. Work to replace the single -lane Kawarau Falls
Bridge near Queenstown with a new two -lane bridge is planned to start in the middle of
this year and I look forward to being part of that. Also, investigation work has been
accelerated for the replacement of the single -lane Motu Bridge near Gisborne as well as
the single-lane Taramakau road-rail bridge on the West Coast of the South Island.
2494 Oral Questions 24 Mar 2015
Denis O’Rourke: When will the Minister come clean with the people of Wellsford ,
Te Hana, and Northland generally that the Government actually has no route through
the Dome Valley and no idea whatsoever when construction could begin on the
Wellsford to Warkworth section of the new motorway?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: The member is talking nonsense. We have been over this
last week and it is old news. I will not rehearse the arguments, suffice to say that we on
this side of the House know that we back the regions with, in fact, billions of dollars’
worth of projects that ma tter in those regions, whereas on the Opposition side all we
hear is carping, because outside of two or three main cities they do not care.
Denis O ’Rourke: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This question was
specifically—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat.
[Interruption] The member will—[Interruption] I have got a very good mind to ask that
member to leave the Chamber, but I will not because he would get an advantage on the
rest of us to, actually, watch the cricket. When the member starts a question with “Why
won’t the Minister come clean”, he can expect the sort of answer he got. He would be
better after question time to go back and make his questions far more concise and
without that sort of innuendo.
GCSB—World Trade Organization Director-General Role
8. DAVID SHEARER (Labour—Mt Albert) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by his quote regarding Hon Tim Groser’s bid to be Director-General of the World Trade
Organisation that if “he decided to put his name in the ring then the New Zealand
Government would give him 100 percent support”; if so, precisely what support did the
Government provide to Mr Groser?
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Attorney -General) on behalf of the  Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: Yes. The Prime Minister also stands by a very similar statement that he made
in 2009 that Helen Clark had all the support of the New Zealand Government as a
candidate to head the United Nations Development Programme. The Government’s
support for Mr Groser included lobbying other leaders for support, New Zealand
missions promoting his campaign, and assistanc e with developing key messages and a
campaign strategy. A lot of resources were used to back Mr Groser’s bid, just as they
were used to back Helen Clark’s bid. We were, of course, all delighted that Helen Clark
was successful, but, sadly, Mr Groser was not successful.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: As the Prime Minister and the Minister for National Security and
Intelligence, would he expect to be briefed if the Government Communications Security
Bureau (GCSB) was undertaking intelligence gathering on behal f of a Minister in his
Cabinet?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: The answer to that would be yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: What reports did the GCSB provide to the Prime Minister in relation
to Tim Groser’s bid for the World Trade Organization (WTO) job?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: It has been the policy of successive
Governments, both National and Labour, not to comment on operational aspects of the
work of the intelligence agencies, because it is not in the public interest to do so.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Will he agree to authorise the Inspector -General of Intelligence and
Security to investigate the GCSB’s activity of the alleged spying on candidates vying
for the WTO role a nd to report her findings either publicly or to the Intelligence and
Security Committee?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: The Prime Minister does not need to instruct
the inspector-general or ask the inspector -general to do anything. The inspector -general
24 Mar 2015 Oral Questions 2495
has wide-ranging powers, many of which came through the 2013 amendments to her
legislation. So if she wants to investigate any matter, she has the ability to do so.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: On what basis did he say that Korea “d oesn’t give a monkey’s”
about New Zealand spying on one of their nationals, and, as Prime Minister, does he
give a monkey’s about foreign powers spying on our Cabinet Ministers?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from David Shearer seeking to debate under
Standing Order 389 the release of a document showing that the Government
Communications Security Bureau undertook targeted monitoring of international
diplomats to support the application of the Hon Tim Groser for the position of Director -
General of the World Trade Organization.
In ruling on an application for an urgent debate, the Speaker has to determine
whether there is a particular case of recent occurrence involving ministerial
responsibility. If something occurs in secret, it may become a case of recent occurrence
for the purpose of the Standing Orders when it becomes publicly known. But the release
upon which this application is based does not involve ministerial responsibility. The
release was by news site, from leaked documents. An urgent debate cannot be granted
on the basis of newspaper allegations or speculation. There must be a distinct
Governmental responsibility for the particular case that  it is seeking to debate. On this
basis, the case raised does not meet the test for me to set aside the business of the House
today. The application is therefore declined.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I thank you

Government refuses to answer que stions as to whether the allegations are correct. I

whether the Government can effectively stonewall, as to whether these allegations made
are correct, by claiming pub lic interest, because, as it currently stands, if it can do so
then the Opposition cannot hold the Government to account in Parliament, which would
be the wrong outcome.

opportunity—with regard to security matters —to say that it is not in the interests of the
country to publicly debate such matters or to answer such questions. So I will certainly
do my best to balance that. I appreciate the point that the Hon David Parker is making.
